title: What If You Jumped on a 300 km/h Train? | What If #7
simplified: Simplified model: the 'frozen' jumper is a labelled thought experiment (in reality nothing can stop her forward motion in mid-air); air drag inside the carriage is ignored because the air moves with the train; distances are rounded.

hook_candidates.text: This train's doing three hundred. Why doesn't she fly back?
Jump on a speeding train and you land where you started.
You've jumped on a moving bus. Why didn't the back wall hit you?
Half a second in the air. The floor moves forty metres.
Watch her feet. She has to land on this red line.

parts.text: She's in the air half a second.
and the back wall slams into her.
parts.tts: and the back wall slams into her!

parts.text: She was already doing three hundred.
so she lands where she left.
at the equator, the ground spins faster than a jet.
parts.tts: At the equator, the ground spins... faster than a jet!

sources: Train speed 300 km/h: UIC High Speed Rail brochure (2018), timeline: 'The Atlantic TGV operates at 300 km/h'; UIC: 'a commercial speed of 250 km/h [is] the principal criterion for the definition of HSR'. https://www.uic.org/com/IMG/pdf/uic_high_speed_brochure.pdf
Half a second in the air: projectile time for a jump about 30 cm high, t = 2*sqrt(2h/g) = 2*sqrt(0.6/9.81) = 0.49 s (standard kinematics).
Shown, not spoken: floor travels 300 km/h = 83.3 m/s x 0.5 s = about 42 m (about two carriages; illustrated as a ruler).

Newton's first law: 'every object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change its state by the action of an external force.' NASA Glenn Research Center, https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/BGP/newton1.html

You keep your sideways speed when you jump: 'When you jump, you pick up some upward velocity, but that does nothing to reduce your sideways velocity. So you continue to east.' University of Illinois Physics Van, https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/18196

Ground speed at the equator: 'the rotational speed of the surface of the earth is more like v = 465 meters per second' = about 1,670 km/h. University of Illinois Physics Van (above). Shown on screen, not spoken.
Faster than a jet: Boeing 787-9 cruise TAS 490 kt (Mach 0.85) = about 907 km/h. SKYbrary B789, https://skybrary.aero/aircraft/b789
comment_question: Have you ever jumped on a moving bus or train to test this?
